chapter: New York bands and the first records
title: First sessions for Hammond: 'Surrender Dear' and 'Bughouse'
summary: His first dates used Teddy Wilson, Charlie Barnet, Jack Jenney, Chu Berry, Bunny Berigan, Gene Krupa and George Van Eps; Norvo notes most became leaders.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: So I -- I don't know, I just kind of forgot about them, but anyway I turned my mind to making these other records. So John -- we got kind of together on the thing and so that's when I made oh, the first record that I had with Surrender Dear -- I used Teddy --
-- and Charlie Barnet, ah, Varn Epps,
I've got the Chicago thing here.
I heard Jack Jenny with Phil Harris's band -- I heard him. Impressed me very much, up at the Astor Roof. He was the third trombone player --
I heard him play when Phil went off the stand, so I was impressed with his playing, so I got him and John liked him -- and had heard him and liked him.
Yeah. He had a very pretty tone and he moved around with -- with ease, didn't he?
He was a very easy trombone player.
But he played very different than -- than I'd heard. Like Miff Mole or Jack Teagarden or
But -- so we did the first date and then we did a second date and we used Bunny Berigan, Jack Jenney, Chu Berry, Johnny Mince. I think --
-- or Artie Shaw, on that date, I think. Or did we use Johnny Mince on the first date?
Johnny Mince used on the first date, when you made HOneysuckle -- no that was the second date, wasn't it? Here --
Well Bughouse was the second date, and Surrender Dear was the first.
Bughouse was the second, well you had Johnny Mince on that one.
And we had Chu Berry, instead of Charlie Barnet --
George Van Eps, you had and Artie Bernstein.
No arrangements, we just did heads.
You did Blues in E-Flat in that one.
Yeah. Do you realize that most of those fellas became leaders?
Yeah, of course, so they did --
Think of the amount of leaders?
I think Benny's date was 'Oh, Pappy,' what he did with Jack Teagarden, I think. And Mildred did a date
-- I think she used Bunny and Johnny Hodges --
-- and Teddy Wilson and a bass player.
Yes she did -- yeah. I think --
I think Stanley said that Mildred's were in here, too. There's pages of your stuff, here, Red. Ah -- well anyway, so that had terrific impact, didn't it -- those?
Yeah. But that was in the early '30's, that was the first date which led later to the idea of getting of me getting a sextet on 52nd Street. So -- I just went back to that, on account of the --
